entries.subject: One open eighteenth-century folding inoculation lancet, backed by one folded white linen cloth.
entries.brief: One OPEN EIGHTEENTH-CENTURY FOLDING LANCET dominates the image diagonally: a small narrow neutral-steel pointed double-edged blade, connected by one clear hinge to a mottled warm dark-brown tortoiseshell handle. Blade slender and short, NOT a syringe, vaccination gun, hypodermic needle or kitchen knife. One folded off-white linen cloth tucked behind the lower half gives a compact supporting mass and a medical-care context, with no blood, wounds or human body. The sharp tip is intact with broad margins. This represents inoculation networks conceptually; do not claim the general-purpose lancet is a specific certified variolation relic.

refs.title: 18th-century lancet in tortoiseshell sheath — Science Museum Group
refs.note: 1701–1800; steel and tortoiseshell. Shape/material reference only; generic lancet, not certified variolation specimen.

refs.title: Vaccination knife — Hong Kong Medical Museum historical collection
refs.note: Historical distinction between variolation and vaccination; no modern injection instrument.

entries.subject: A historical horn-handled single-blade veterinary fleam across a horseshoe.
entries.brief: One SINGLE-BLADED HISTORICAL VETERINARY FLEAM is laid diagonally across ONE plain broad iron horseshoe. A warm brown curved horn handle, clear hinge, and one blunt-tipped steel blade with its characteristic small perpendicular triangular cutting point at the side: NOT a modern scalpel or multi-tool. The horseshoe opens upward and has a few broad nail holes. Natural iron grey, horn brown, neutral ivory highlights; no blue cast, no blood. The veterinary instrument should be as prominent as the horseshoe, so it means animal medicine, not only forging or selective breeding. Historically-informed conceptual icon, no modern veterinary cross, stethoscope or electric gadget.

refs.title: Fleam, single bladed — Science Museum Group
refs.note: 1750–1850, William Pepys; steel and horn. Catalogue consulted; image search also found later related fleams.

refs.title: History of veterinary practice — RCVS
refs.note: Documents the relation to farriery and the development of veterinary schools.

entries.subject: Open nineteenth-century portable vaccination case with grouped glass tubes and one ivory-handled lancet.
entries.brief: ONE OPEN NINETEENTH-CENTURY PORTABLE VACCINATION CASE dominates the icon, oblong warm brown leather exterior, hinged lid open, dark subdued red-brown velvet interior. Within it, FOUR MATCHING slender clear glass vaccine tubes lie neatly in fitted parallel channels, with restrained pale contents and realistic closed ends, unlabelled. ONE ivory-handled narrow steel vaccination lancet lies in its own wider fitted channel beside the tubes. Repeated supplies and an organised portable kit communicate a campaign, not a single inoculation. No extra instruments, medical logo, readable labels, modern plastic caps, hypodermic syringe or bifurcated needle. The nineteenth-century museum kit informs materials; the repeated tubes are a conceptual adaptation, NOT an exact replica.

refs.title: Vaccination lancet, glass tube and bandage — Science Museum Group
refs.note: 1801–1900; ivory/steel lancet, glass tube and leather case. Four tubes are an icon adaptation rather than catalogue inventory.
